summary: The evidence does not support that vitamin C prevents the common cold for the general population. Large Cochrane reviews consistently find little to no reduction in cold incidence in everyday use. Vitamin C may modestly shorten duration and has clearer preventive effects only in specific high-physical-stress groups.

sources.title: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
sources.quote: Regular supplementation had no effect on common cold incidence in the ordinary community.
sources.credibility_reason: Cochrane systematic review with high methodological rigor and broad evidence base.

sources.title: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin C
sources.quote: Routine vitamin C supplementation does not reduce the risk of developing colds in most people.
sources.credibility_reason: Official U.S. government health resource synthesizing high-quality evidence.

sources.title: Mayo Clinic: Vitamin C
sources.quote: For most people, vitamin C supplements don't prevent colds, though they may slightly shorten duration.
sources.credibility_reason: Trusted clinical institution with evidence-aligned patient guidance.

sources.title: Vitamin C and infections under physical stress
sources.quote: In marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions, incidence was reduced by half.
sources.credibility_reason: Peer-reviewed evidence with clear subgroup effects but limited generalizability.

sources.title: CDC: Vitamin C overview
sources.quote: Vitamin C is essential for immune function, but supplementation has limited preventive effect on common cold incidence.
sources.credibility_reason: Government public-health source consistent with major review findings.
